procedural_history.impugned_order: Order made by the District Magistrate, Karnal under s. 3 of the Preventive Detention Act on the August 18, 1957, and which was approved by the State Government on August 29, 1957.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Original Jurisdiction: Petition No. 135 of 1957(xii) under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ in the nature of habeas corpus.

directions: a writ be issued as prayed for
the petitioner be set at liberty forthwith

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure of the Advisory Board to submit its report within the ten-week period prescribed by Section 10 of the Preventive Detention Act renders the subsequent detention of the petitioner illegal.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the Preventive Detention Act on August 18, 1957.
The petitioner alleged that the Advisory Board had not submitted its report concerning his detention.
The ten-week period for the Board to submit its report, as required by the Act, expired on October 27, 1957.
The State Government, in its counter-affidavits, did not deny or address the petitioner's allegation that the report was not submitted within the prescribed time.
law: Section 10 of the Preventive Detention Act requires the Advisory Board to submit its report to the State Government within ten weeks from the date of detention.

Section 11 of the Act requires the government to act upon the report. If the report is against detention, the government must release the person "forthwith". If it approves detention, the government must make a fresh decision on whether to continue the detention and for how long.
application: The Court reasoned that the ten-week time limit for the Advisory Board's report is of the "utmost importance" to the person being detained (the detenu).

A delay in submitting the report harms the detenu in either scenario: if the report recommends release, the delay unlawfully prolongs their detention; if the report approves detention, the delay deprives the detenu of a timely and fresh decision by the government about the continuation of their detention.
The Court concluded that the time limit is a mandatory requirement of the procedure established by law.
Since the petitioner specifically alleged that the report was not submitted in time and the State failed to challenge this fact in its affidavits, the Court accepted the allegation as true.
Therefore, the Court found that the petitioner's detention became illegal after the ten-week period expired on October 27, 1957, because the mandatory procedure was not followed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the failure of the Advisory Board to submit its report within the ten-week period prescribed by Section 10 of the Preventive Detention Act is a violation of the procedure established by law. This failure renders any detention beyond that ten-week period illegal and unlawful.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure of the Advisory Board to submit its report within the ten-week period prescribed by Section 10 of the Preventive Detention Act renders the subsequent detention of the petitioner illegal.
appellant_arguments: The Advisory Board was required to submit its report within ten weeks of the petitioner's detention, a period which expired on October 27, 1957.
The Board failed to submit its report within this prescribed period.
As a result of this failure, the petitioner's detention from October 28, 1957, onwards became illegal and bad.
The failure to adhere to the procedure in Section 10 of the Act means the petitioner has been deprived of his personal liberty otherwise than in accordance with procedure established by law.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner's petition did not explicitly allege that the Board had not submitted its report; it only stated that the Board had not made an 'order'.
Under the Act, the Board's duty is to submit a report, not make an order, and therefore the State was not expected to respond to an allegation that was not properly made.
The State requested an adjournment to get time to ascertain whether the report had been submitted within the deadline.

cases.case_name: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
cases.principle: For determining the essentials of a valid sanction for the prosecution of a public servant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a detenu alleges that the Advisory Board has not submitted its report within the statutorily prescribed ten-week period, and the government fails to controvert this allegation in its counter-affidavit, the detention becomes illegal after the expiration of that period.
obiter: The submission of the Advisory Board's report within the time prescribed by law is of the utmost importance to the detenu.

A delay in the submission of the report may unlawfully prolong the detention, as it can postpone the detenu's release if the report is unfavorable to the detention, or deprive the detenu of a timely fresh decision by the State Government if the report approves the detention.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The submission of the Advisory Board's report within the ten-week period prescribed by Section 10 of the Preventive Detention Act is a critical procedural safeguard. A failure to meet this deadline is a violation of the procedure established by law, as it prejudices the detenu in either case: if the report is against detention, it unlawfully prolongs their confinement; if it approves detention, it deprives the detenu of a timely fresh decision by the State Government on the continuation of their detention. Consequently, any detention beyond the ten-week period without the Board's report becomes illegal.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the detenu has been deprived of his personal liberty otherwise than in accordance with procedure established by law.
why_respondent_won: The court rejected the State's argument that the petitioner's grievance was improperly pleaded because he used the word 'order' instead of 'report'. The court held that since the Board's only duty under the Act is to submit a report, a 'plain reading' of the petition shows that the 'substance' of the grievance was clearly the failure to submit the report within the prescribed period.

The court denied the State's request for an adjournment to ascertain the facts, because the petitioner had 'definitely made' the allegation in his petition, and the State had failed to deal with that specific allegation in either of the two affidavits it had already filed in opposition.

The State failed to controvert the petitioner's factual assertion that the Advisory Board had not submitted its report within the ten-week deadline, leaving the court to accept the petitioner's allegation as true.
policy_considerations: The making of the report within the time prescribed by law is of the utmost importance to the detenu, as the failure to do so may have the effect of unlawfully prolonging the detention.
